sections.b: Ezra opens with the decree that ends Chronicles, now continued: whoever belongs to the LORD's people may go up "and build the house of the LORD, the God of Israel" (Ezra 1:3). Cyrus returns the Temple vessels through his treasurer (Ezra 1:7–11), and the builders appeal to his permission when they buy cedar (Ezra 3:7) and when they turn down outside help (Ezra 4:3). Years later the elders cite his decree to Tattenai (Ezra 5:13–15), and Darius finds his memorandum at Ecbatana, setting the house's size and promising royal funds (Ezra 6:2–5). The book thus rests the Temple's legal standing on Cyrus, and its theological standing on the God who roused him (Ezra 1:1).

common: Ezra preserves two forms of Cyrus's decree, a Hebrew proclamation (1:2–4) and an Aramaic archive memorandum (6:3–5).
uncommon: Some historians think the Hebrew decree was composed by a Jewish writer on the basis of the Aramaic memorandum.

sections.b: Ezra tells the end of the Babylonian exile as a new exodus. God rouses Cyrus and the people (Ezra 1:1, 5), neighbors give silver and gold as Egypt once did (Ezra 1:6), and the Temple vessels come home (Ezra 1:7–11). Chapter 2 counts the families of "the province" who came back, each to its town, and the returnees call themselves "the people of the exile" (Ezra 4:1; Ezra 6:16, 19–21). Babylonian tablets from Al-Yahudu, "Judah-town," show that many Judeans had settled there and stayed, which helps explain why the returning groups were small.

common: The first exiles returned under Cyrus in 538 BC.
uncommon: Many scholars think most families in Ezra 2 came in several waves between 538 and 520 BC or later.

sections.b: Ezra 1–6 tells how the house burned in 586 BC was rebuilt. The altar comes first, in the seventh month (Ezra 3:1–6); the foundation follows with trumpets, cymbals and the refrain of God's loyal love, while old men who remembered Solomon's house weep (Ezra 3:10–13). Opposition stops the work (Ezra 4:1–5, 24) until Haggai and Zechariah stir the builders in 520 BC (Ezra 5:1–2). Darius confirms Cyrus's order and pays the costs (Ezra 6:1–12), and the house is finished on the third of Adar, 515 BC, and dedicated with joy (Ezra 6:15–18). This is the Temple, enlarged by Herod, that stood in Jesus' day.

common: The second Temple was finished in 515 BC, about seventy years after the first was destroyed.
uncommon: Some scholars think the Temple's foundation was laid only once, in 520 BC, and that Ezra 3 dates it earlier.

claude.title: Claude's theory: a house built by permission
claude.body: My own observation: no building in the Bible is surrounded by so much paperwork. Ezra 1–6 quotes a decree, an inventory, accusations, a king's reply, an inspector's report, an archive memo and a royal order. Solomon's Temple was built by a king; this one is built by subjects, and every stone needs a document. The book seems to say that God's house can stand in an empire's world, by God's providence working through the empire's own law. Commentators note the documents' role (Eskenazi calls Ezra–Nehemiah a book about documents); the contrast with Solomon's royal building is my framing.

sections.b: In Ezra 4 people descended from settlers brought by Esarhaddon offer to help build the Temple, saying they have worshiped Israel's God for generations; Zerubbabel and Jeshua refuse (Ezra 4:1–3). "The people of the land" then discourage the builders and write to the Persian court (Ezra 4:4–23). Josephus calls these opponents Cuthaeans and Samaritans, and the story became part of the long Jewish-Samaritan quarrel. Many scholars caution that a distinct Samaritan community with its own temple on Mount Gerizim emerged later, and that Ezra tells only one side. The same chapter's opponents write from Samaria (Ezra 4:10, 17), while Ezra 6:21 shows that some outsiders who separated themselves were welcomed.

common: The adversaries of Ezra 4 are often identified with the Samaritans.
uncommon: Some scholars think the 'people of the land' included many Judeans who had never been exiled.

sections.b: Zerubbabel heads the list of returnees (Ezra 2:2), builds the altar with Jeshua (Ezra 3:2), lays the foundation (Ezra 3:8–10), refuses outside help (Ezra 4:2–3) and starts building again at the prophets' word (Ezra 5:2). Ezra calls him "son of Shealtiel," while 1 Chronicles 3:19 makes him the son of Pedaiah. He is never called governor in Ezra, but Haggai gives him that title (Haggai 1:1), and he is probably the unnamed "governor of the Jews" in Ezra 6:7. He then vanishes from the record, and the Temple is dedicated with no mention of him (Ezra 6:16–18).
sections.refs: Ezra 2:2; Ezra 3:2; Ezra 3:8–10; Ezra 4:2–3; Ezra 5:2; Ezra 6:7; 1 Chronicles 3:19; Haggai 1:1

common: Zerubbabel was a grandson of King Jehoiachin and led the rebuilding of the Temple.
uncommon: Some historians think the Persians removed Zerubbabel because of hopes that he would restore David's kingdom (Haggai 2:21–23).

sections.b: Sheshbazzar receives the counted vessels from Cyrus's treasurer and brings them to Jerusalem (Ezra 1:8–11). The elders later tell Tattenai that Cyrus made him governor and that he laid the foundations (Ezra 5:14–16). The Greek translation of Ezra calls him a treasurer instead (Ezra 5:14), and 1 Esdras names him beside Zerubbabel. He is never mentioned again.

common: Most scholars think Sheshbazzar and Zerubbabel were different men.
uncommon: Some readers identify Sheshbazzar with Zerubbabel, or with Shenazzar son of Jehoiachin (1 Chronicles 3:18).

sections.b: Ezra begins by saying Cyrus's decree fulfilled "the LORD's word from Jeremiah's mouth" (Ezra 1:1), that is, the promise that after seventy years for Babylon God would bring his people back (Jeremiah 29:10). The Temple was finished in 515 BC (Ezra 6:15), about seventy years after it was burned, which fits Zechariah's question about God's anger "these seventy years" (Zechariah 1:12). So the seventy years can be counted to the return (538 BC) or to the rebuilt Temple (515 BC).

The first feast in the finished second Temple is Passover, on the fourteenth of the first month (Ezra 6:19–22). The priests and Levites purify themselves, slaughter the Passover for the people of the exile, and the meal is shared with all who had separated themselves from the nations' uncleanness to seek the LORD. As at Hezekiah's and Josiah's Passovers (2 Chronicles 30; 2 Chronicles 35), the feast seals a restoration, and it marks the return from Babylon as a second exodus.

Ezra's list of returnees counts 128 singers, all "descendants of Asaph," separately from the Levites (Ezra 2:41; Nehemiah 7:44 has 148). At the founding of the Temple the Levites of Asaph's family lead the praise with cymbals "as David king of Israel had arranged," singing "For he is good, for his loyal love over Israel is forever" (Ezra 3:10–11). The singers settle in their towns (Ezra 2:70) and later receive royal tax exemption (Ezra 7:24).

Four priestly families came back with 4,289 men, but only 74 Levites (Ezra 2:36–40). Priests who could not prove their descent were kept from the holy food until a priest could consult the Urim and Thummim (Ezra 2:61–63). Jeshua the high priest, grandson of the last chief priest before the exile, rebuilds the altar with Zerubbabel (Ezra 3:2). Levites from twenty years old oversee the building (Ezra 3:8–9), and at the dedication the priests and Levites are set in their divisions "according to what is written in the book of Moses" (Ezra 6:18).

Ezra 1–6 is full of the Persian empire's machinery: a royal decree (Ezra 1:2–4), a treasurer with a Persian title (Ezra 1:8), a province called Beyond the River and its governor Tattenai, known from a Babylonian tablet (Ezra 5:3), letters in the official Aramaic (Ezra 4:8–6:18), searches of royal archives (Ezra 4:15, 19; Ezra 6:1–2), taxes called tribute, tax and duty (Ezra 4:13, 20), and the threat of impalement (Ezra 6:11). The kings named are Cyrus, Darius I, Ahasuerus (Xerxes I) and Artaxerxes I, though not in time order (Ezra 4:5–24).

From Ezra 4:8 to 6:18 the book is written in Aramaic, and again in Artaxerxes' letter of Ezra 7:12–26. The letters keep Aramaic letter form: address, greeting ("Peace"), "and now," and the body (Ezra 4:11, 17; Ezra 5:7). The narrator also tells the story between the documents in Aramaic (Ezra 4:23–5:5; Ezra 6:13–18). Ezra 4:7 marks the switch, saying the letter was written in Aramaic script and translated into Aramaic.

Ezra credits Haggai, with Zechariah, for restarting the Temple in Darius's second year (Ezra 5:1–2) and for its completion (Ezra 6:14). Haggai's own book dates the restart to the twenty-fourth of the sixth month, 520 BC (Haggai 1:14–15), and speaks to the old men who compared the new house with Solomon's (Haggai 2:3; compare Ezra 3:12).

Ezra calls the prophet "Zechariah son of Iddo" and pairs him with Haggai in restarting and finishing the Temple (Ezra 5:1; Ezra 6:14). His book promises that "Zerubbabel's own hands founded this house, and his hands will bring it to completion" (Zechariah 4:9), which readers see fulfilled when the house is finished (Ezra 6:15), though Ezra does not name Zerubbabel there.

1 Esdras parallels Ezra 1–6 closely but in a different order: Cyrus's decree and the vessels (1 Esdras 2:1–15), then the Artaxerxes letters of Ezra 4:7–24 (1 Esdras 2:16–30), then the story of Darius's three guards, where Zerubbabel wins leave to rebuild (1 Esdras 3:1–5:6), and only then the list of returnees (1 Esdras 5:7–46). Its numbers sometimes differ: the vessel totals add up (1 Esdras 2:13–14), and it dates the completion to the twenty-third of Adar (1 Esdras 7:5). Verse numbers here follow the KJV Apocrypha; Rahlfs' Greek numbers some verses differently.

Ezra 2, repeated in Nehemiah 7, lists those who came back by family, by town and by clergy. Its purpose is to say who belongs: priests without records are set aside (Ezra 2:62), and families who cannot show they are from Israel are listed apart (Ezra 2:59–60). The numbers add to 29,818, while the total given is 42,360 (Ezra 2:64).

sections.h: Waiting for the Urim and Thummim
sections.b: After the exile the governor ruled that priests who could not prove their descent should not eat the most holy food "until a priest arose who could use the Urim and the Thummim" (Ezra 2:63; Nehemiah 7:65). The ruling assumes the sacred lots were no longer in use. Jewish tradition says they never returned (Mishnah Sotah 9:12; Bavli Yoma 21b).

In the first autumn after the return, the people kept the Feast of Booths "just as it is written," with the daily burnt offerings Numbers 29 prescribes, even before the Temple was founded (Ezra 3:4–6).

sections.h: Twelve tribes in a small community
sections.b: Though the returnees came mainly from Judah, Benjamin and Levi (Ezra 1:5), they dedicated the Temple with twelve goats "for all Israel, matching the number of Israel's tribes" (Ezra 6:17), and their list may once have named twelve leaders (Ezra 2:2; Nehemiah 7:7).

sections.h: The God who made his name live there
sections.b: Cyrus calls Israel's God "the God who is in Jerusalem" (Ezra 1:3), and Darius's decree calls on "the God who has made his name live there" (Ezra 6:12), the phrase of Deuteronomy 12:11.

The Passover of Ezra 6:21 was eaten by the returned exiles "along with everyone who had separated himself to them from the uncleanness of the nations of the land." Whether these were converts or Judeans who had never been exiled, the verse shows a community open to those who committed themselves to the LORD, just after it had refused partnership with others (Ezra 4:3).

Ezra 1–6 keeps naming God as the hidden actor in Persian politics: he rouses Cyrus's spirit (Ezra 1:1), keeps his eye on the elders while a report goes to Darius (Ezra 5:5), and turns "the Assyrian king's heart" toward his people (Ezra 6:22).

The return from Babylon is told with exodus colors: neighbors give silver and gold (Ezra 1:4–6; Exodus 12:35–36), the sacred vessels travel with the people (Ezra 1:7–11; Isaiah 52:11–12), and the story of the rebuilt Temple ends with Passover and the Feast of Unleavened Bread (Ezra 6:19–22).
